title: Saxon Course 2 · Lessons 11–15 · finding the variable
vocabLabel: The way the book puts it
bigQuestion: 1. Find the part you don’t like.   2. Undo it — on <u>both</u> sides.   3. Cross it out and solve.
eyebrow: Saxon Math Course 2 · Lessons 11–15 · before tomorrow's test
foot: Practice questions written for this review. Every number is different from the homework's, and nothing from the textbook is reproduced here. Skills, method, vocabulary and lesson numbers follow Saxon Math, Course 2 (Stephen Hake).
note:
/* Built for the test on Lessons 11–15, from four problems that came back
   wrong: Lesson 12 problem 14, and Lesson 14 problems 4, 8 and 12. Three of
   the four are the same skill wearing different clothes — a variable with a
   number stuck to it — so eight of the twelve questions ask which move undoes
   the number rather than what the answer is. That is the step he is missing;
   the arithmetic was never the problem. Two questions then solve one through
   to the end, and two are the Property of Zero for Multiplication, which is
   problem 8 and is simply a thing to remember.

   "Undo" is the book's own word, not ours: Lesson 2 says addition and
   subtraction are inverse operations and that we can "undo" an addition by
   subtracting one addend from the sum. Every number here is different from
   the homework's and from the book's worked examples. */

sets.name: Which Part Don't You Like?
sets.blurb: Four equations. Don't solve them — just name the move that undoes the number stuck to the variable.

items.q:
n − 1846 = 2375
Which move undoes the 1846? Don't solve it — just name the move.
items.why: The part you don't like is the − 1846. It was taken away from n, so adding 1846 puts it back — and it goes on both sides. That leaves n = 2375 + 1846 = 4221. Check it: 4221 − 1846 = 2375. ✓
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown numbers in subtraction

items.why: 268 was added on, so subtracting 268 takes it back off — both sides. c = 900 − 268 = 632. Check it: 632 + 268 = 900. ✓
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown numbers in addition

items.why: 14p means 14 times p, so the 14 is multiplying. Dividing by 14 undoes that, on both sides. p = $3.36 ÷ 14 = $0.24. Check it: 14 × $0.24 = $3.36. ✓ Nothing is being added here, so adding and subtracting cannot help.
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown factors

items.why: m was cut into 18 parts. Multiplying by 18 puts it back together, on both sides. m = 24 × 18 = 432. Check it: 432 ÷ 18 = 24. ✓ Dividing again is the commonest slip — it makes the variable smaller when it needs to get bigger.
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown numbers in division

sets.name: Undo It on Both Sides
sets.blurb: Naming the move is half of it. These are the four ways it goes wrong afterwards.

items.hi: If you take 85 off one side and not the other, the promise is broken
items.q: Priya has k + 85 = 240. She crosses the 85 off the left side and writes k = 240. What went wrong?
opts: She took the 85 off one side only
She should have added 85 to both sides
She should have divided both sides by 85
Nothing — k = 240 is the right answer
items.why: Crossing out is the last step, not the first. The 85 only disappears because you subtracted it — and a subtraction has to happen on both sides or the equation stops being true. k = 240 − 85 = 155. Check it: 155 + 85 = 240. ✓ Her answer of 240 fails that check straight away: 240 + 85 = 325, not 240.
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown numbers in addition

items.hi: if they do not, the undo went the wrong way
items.q: Ana has b − 512 = 349. She subtracts 512 from both sides. Is that the move?
opts: No — 512 was taken away, so add it back
Yes — subtracting is how you clear a number
No — divide both sides by 512 instead
No — multiply both sides by 512 instead
items.why: She did do it to both sides, which is right — but she did the same thing again instead of the opposite. The 512 is already being subtracted, so adding is what undoes it. b = 349 + 512 = 861. Check it: 861 − 512 = 349. ✓ Her way gives b = −163, and −163 − 512 is nowhere near 349.
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown numbers in subtraction

items.hi: multiply those numbers together first so there is only one left to undo
items.q:
4 · 3g = 8400
Two numbers are multiplying g, so multiply them together first: 4 · 3 is 12, and the equation is really 12g = 8400.
Now — which move undoes the 12?
items.why: 4 · 3g means 4 × 3 × g, and 4 × 3 is just 12 — so tidy that up first and there is one number stuck to g instead of two. The 12 is multiplying, so divide both sides by 12: g = 8400 ÷ 12 = 700. Check it: 4 · 3 · 700 = 8400. ✓
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown factors

items.hi: Whatever you do, do it to both sides.
items.why: $1.75 is added on, so subtract $1.75 from both sides: q = $6.00 − $1.75 = $4.25. Check it: $1.75 + $4.25 = $6.00. ✓ $7.75 is what you get by adding instead of subtracting — the right number, the wrong direction.
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown numbers in addition

sets.tag: Aimed at L12 #14, and the kind that reads backwards
sets.name: Cross It Out and Solve
sets.blurb: All three steps, end to end — and the one shape where the rule is different.

items.why: w is divided by 30, so multiply both sides by 30: w = 14 × 30 = 420. Check it: 420 ÷ 30 = 14. ✓ 44 comes from adding and 16 from subtracting — neither undoes a division.
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown numbers in division

items.hi: To find an unknown subtrahend, subtract the difference from the minuend.
items.q:
Careful — here the variable is the part being taken away.
$50.00 − h = $11.40
What is h?
items.why: In b − 512 = 349 the variable is what you start with, so you add. Here it is the part being taken away — the subtrahend — so you subtract the difference from the minuend: $50.00 − $11.40 = $38.60. Check it: $50.00 − $38.60 = $11.40. ✓ $61.40 is adding out of habit, and it fails the check immediately.
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown numbers in subtraction
items.kind: the variable is the part taken away

sets.name: The Property of Zero
sets.blurb: Nothing to undo here. This one is simply a thing to remember, and its three neighbours are what make it easy to miss.

items.hi: there is a zero among the factors, so the product is zero
opts: The Property of Zero for Multiplication
items.why: One of the factors is zero, so the whole product is zero — you never have to multiply the 6, the 4 and the 3 at all. The book calls this the Property of Zero for Multiplication; other books call it the Zero Property of Multiplication, and they are the same rule.
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 2 — properties of operations

items.hi: The Identity Property of Multiplication is about one, not zero
items.q: Which equation shows the Property of Zero for Multiplication?
items.why: Multiplying by zero gives zero. The other three are its neighbours, and they are the ones worth telling apart: 7 · 1 = 7 is the Identity Property of Multiplication (about one), 7 + 0 = 7 is the Identity Property of Addition (zero, but added rather than multiplied), and 7 · 2 = 2 · 7 is the Commutative Property — the order of the factors.
items.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 2 — properties of operations

build.q: Pick the two equations that are solved by dividing both sides by 12.
build.hit: Both of those come undone by dividing by 12.
build.answer: Dividing by 12 undoes multiplying by 12. 12t = 96 gives t = 8, and 4 · 3g = 8400 is 12g = 8400 once the factors are multiplied out, so g = 700. The others had something else done to the variable, so they come undone some other way: t − 12 = 96 has 12 added back, t + 12 = 96 has 12 subtracted, t ÷ 12 = 96 is multiplied by 12, and 12 − t = 96 has the variable as the part taken away.
build.cite: Saxon Math Course 2, Lesson 3 — unknown numbers

steps.title: The three steps
steps.book: Lesson 3 works one equation of each kind, on pages 21 and 22.
text: Step one. Look at the side the variable is on and find the part you do not like. It is the number stuck to the variable — added on to it, taken away from it, multiplying it, or dividing it. That number is the only thing standing between you and the answer.

Step two. Undo it. Addition and subtraction are inverse operations, so adding undoes subtracting and subtracting undoes adding. Multiplication and division are inverse operations too, so dividing undoes multiplying and multiplying undoes dividing. Whatever you do, do it to both sides.

Step three. Cross it out. The part you did not like has gone, the variable is standing on its own, and whatever is left on the other side is the answer. Then put that answer back into the equation you started with and check it.
One extra. If more than one number is multiplying the variable, as in 4 · 3g, multiply those numbers together first so there is only one left to undo.
vocab: Two operations that undo each other. Addition and subtraction are a pair; multiplication and division are a pair.
A number being added. An unknown addend is found by subtracting.
A number being multiplied. An unknown factor is found by dividing the product by the known factor.

both.title: Both sides, always
both.book: Lesson 3 checks every answer this way; see the worked examples on page 21.
text: An equation says that the two sides are equal, and the equals sign is a promise. If you take 85 off one side and not the other, the promise is broken and what is left is no longer true.
So an undo is never done to one side. It is done to both, at the same moment, with the same number. That is what keeps the two sides level while the part you did not like disappears.

Doing it to both sides is not the same as doing the same operation twice. If a number is being subtracted, you add it back; adding it to one side and subtracting it from the other is not balancing, it is two different moves.

The check is free and it catches everything. Put your answer back where the variable was and work the arithmetic out. If both sides come out the same, you are right; if they do not, the undo went the wrong way.
vocab: A statement that two amounts are equal.
Both sides changed the same way, so they stay equal.

minuend.title: When the variable is the part taken away
minuend.book: Lesson 3 names all three parts and works one of each, on page 21.
text: A subtraction has three parts. The number you start with is the minuend, the number taken away is the subtrahend, and what is left over is the difference: minuend − subtrahend = difference.
Nearly all of the practice has an unknown minuend, like b − 512 = 349. The variable is the number you started with, some of it was taken away, and to get it back you add the other two numbers.

This one is the other kind. In $50.00 − h = $11.40 the variable is the subtrahend — it is the part being taken away, not the amount you started with. To find an unknown subtrahend, subtract the difference from the minuend.

The quickest way to tell them apart is to look at which side of the minus sign the variable is on. On the left it is the minuend, so add. On the right it is the subtrahend, so subtract. Either way, check by putting the answer back and doing the subtraction.
vocab: The number you start with, on the left of the minus sign.
The number being taken away, on the right of the minus sign.
What is left after the subtraction.

zero.title: The Property of Zero for Multiplication
zero.book: Lesson 2 lists the properties side by side, on pages 14 and 15.
text: The Property of Zero for Multiplication says that any number multiplied by zero is zero. The book writes it as a · 0 = 0. Other books call it the Zero Property of Multiplication; it is the same rule under a different name.
It does not matter how long the string of factors is. In 6 · 4 · 3 · 0 there is a zero among the factors, so the product is zero and the rest of the multiplying never has to be done.

The reason it is easy to miss is that it has three close neighbours. The Identity Property of Multiplication is about one, not zero: a · 1 = a. The Identity Property of Addition is about zero but adds it instead of multiplying: a + 0 = a. The Commutative Property is about the order of the factors: a · b = b · a.
So when a question shows an equation and asks for the property, read two things: which operation it is, and which number is doing the work — a zero or a one.
vocab: The number that leaves another number unchanged: 0 for adding, 1 for multiplying.
